  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action

Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Status:** Internal advice – privileged
**Basis:** Seller update draft and Disclosure Letter dated 22 September 2026, reviewed against the Wattlebridge Negotiation Playbook. The Seller's description of positions as "negotiated", "agreed", "settled", "adequate" or "fair and balanced" has been disregarded per playbook §0.4/§6.3 – nothing in the Seller's package has been through our authority process.

---

## 1. Headline assessment

The Seller's draft departs from our playbook on essentially every protection item. The pattern is consistent: the Seller moves every number to its end of the range, collapses the separate Fundamental/Tax/IP regimes into the general cap, and then layers on three further erosions (blanket buyer-knowledge bar, whole-data-room deemed disclosure, "all Claims" override). Read together, Clauses 8.3, 12.3 and 9.3/12.8/20.5 plus Schedule 7 would, in practice, leave the warranty package with very little recoverable value and would purport to strip out even fraud.

Separately, the Disclosure Letter is actually useful to us: in its own words it confirms that the Bluefen consent, Riverlark payout, Ironquay assignment and bonus funding are all **unresolved** at the date of the letter. We should hold the Seller to those admissions.

**Nothing in this package can be accepted as drafted.** Several items require escalation to Amelia Frost because the Seller is pitching at our fallback numbers – but no fallback authority has been given, and matching a number is not clearance.

---

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### 2.1 General warranty cap – Clause 12.1

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Cap | 20% / AUD 4,800,000 | 25% / AUD 6,000,000 starting position |

**Reasoning.** The Seller's 20% figure coincides exactly with our conditional fallback. That is precisely the situation playbook §0.4 warns about: a match to a fallback number does not clear the position. The fallback is usable **only** with prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft, and none exists. We also should not spend the fallback at this stage – the Seller has made no concessions elsewhere, so conceding the cap would be a unilateral give.

**Position.** Mark back to 25% / AUD 6,000,000. Do not signal that 20% is available. If the team wants to table 20% at a later stage as part of a package (e.g. in exchange for a full fundamental regime, 24 months and proper disclosure), obtain Amelia Frost's written approval first, referencing the specific draft.

### 2.2 Thresholds – Clause 12.2

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 |
| Basket | AUD 250,000 | AUD 50,000 |
| Recovery once exceeded | Excess only (deductible) | First dollar (tipping) |

**Reasoning.** These are five-times multiples of our figures and the Seller has also converted the basket from a tipping basket to a deductible. Combined with the AUD 25,000 de minimis, a business with ~AUD 12m revenue could have a material number of genuine warranty breaches (individual contract, employee, data issues) that are individually excluded and collectively never reach the basket. The deductible mechanism alone costs us AUD 250,000 on any claim that does qualify.

**Position.** Reject all three. Restate de minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; seller liable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded. Confirm expressly that the de minimis and basket do not apply to Fundamental/Title claims, Tax, specific indemnities or fraud (see 2.4 and 2.5).

### 2.3 Time limits and "all Claims" override – Clauses 12.3 / 13

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| General claims period | 18 months | 24 months (18 is fallback – no approval given) |
| Scope language | Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise | Keep categories separate; no hidden general-regime override |

**Reasoning – 18 months.** Same analysis as the cap: the Seller has landed on our fallback number, no Amelia Frost approval exists, and 18 months is particularly weak here because the first post-completion audit cycle (which is where accounts and tax warranty issues typically surface) will not have fully run by then. Mark back to 24 months.

**Reasoning – "all Claims" default.** This sentence is the most dangerous drafting in the package. A default rule that every limitation applies to every Claim "unless expressly stated otherwise" inverts the normal structure: instead of the Seller needing to justify each limitation, the Buyer has to find and carve out every category individually, and any gap in our drafting silently sweeps Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, payment covenants and even fraud into the 18-month / 20% / basket regime. This is the "hidden general-regime override" our playbook specifically prohibits.

**Position.** Delete the default rule. Replace with the reverse: limitations in Clause 12 apply **only** to General Warranty Claims, and each other category (Fundamental/Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, covenants, leakage/price adjustment) is governed solely by its own stated regime.

### 2.4 Fundamental / Title warranties

**Seller:** capacity and title warranties subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties "for administrative simplicity."

**Playbook:** separate regime – 100% of price cap, minimum six years, outside basket, de minimis and any knowledge bar.

**Reasoning.** "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason. If the Seller does not own the shares or lacks capacity to sell, the Buyer has paid AUD 24m for nothing; a 20% cap would leave AUD 19.2m unrecoverable, and an 18-month window could expire before a title defect (e.g. an unregistered charge or a prior transfer) emerges. This is an unconditional playbook position with no fallback.

**Position.** Reject outright. Fundamental/Title Warranties: cap equal to the purchase price (100%), claims period not less than six years, expressly excluded from Clauses 12.2 (thresholds), 8.3 (knowledge) and the Schedule 7 general disclosure.

### 2.5 Exclusive remedy and non-reliance – Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5

**Seller:** limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply "to all Claims of any nature."

**Playbook:** fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable; no one may waive this.

**Reasoning.** As drafted, the Seller's language would purport to cap and time-bar fraud claims and to have the Buyer disclaim reliance on fraudulent statements. Apart from being unacceptable commercially, a clause purporting to exclude liability for one's own fraud is of doubtful enforceability under NSW law, but we should not rely on a court striking it down – the clause must carry the carve-out expressly. The "all Claims of any nature" wording also reinforces the override problem in 2.3 by pulling specific indemnities and Tax into the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance net.

**Position.** Insert an express, non-waivable carve-out: nothing in the Agreement limits or excludes liability for fraud, wilful concealment or deliberate misconduct of the Seller, the Company or any of their officers, and the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses do not apply to such matters. Restrict the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses to General Warranty Claims only. This is a non-negotiable item and does not require escalation to accept – it requires escalation only if the deal team is contemplating departing from it, which it should not.

### 2.6 Disclosure – Schedule 7 and Disclosure Letter paras 1.1 / 1.2

**Seller:** general disclosure of the entire data room as at 5pm 22 September 2026 (DD-002 to DD-012), the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records."

**Playbook:** specific fair disclosure only; reject whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search deemed disclosure.

**Reasoning.** Whole-data-room disclosure converts every document into a qualification of every warranty regardless of whether its relevance was apparent. Public-register disclosure is worse – it qualifies warranties by reference to material that was never in the data room and that the Buyer may not have searched. Combined with Clause 8.3 (which separately bars claims for matters "discoverable from" the data room or public records), the Seller gets two bites: anything in the data room is both disclosed and deemed known. The Disclosure Letter's para 1.4 ("nothing admits … that any consent, payment, notice … is legally required") also means the Seller is seeking the benefit of disclosure while refusing to characterise what has been disclosed.

**Position.** Delete paras 1.1 and 1.2 as general disclosures. Replace with: the Warranties are qualified only by matters **fairly disclosed** in the Disclosure Letter with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Documents in the data room qualify warranties only where specifically cross-referenced against the relevant warranty. No disclosure by reference to public registers or a notional prudent-search standard. Fundamental/Title and Tax warranties should not be qualified by general disclosure at all.

### 2.7 Buyer knowledge – Clause 8.3

**Seller:** no claim for any matter of which the Buyer "or its advisers" had knowledge, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

**Playbook:** delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; any qualifier limited to actual knowledge of named persons, with a reasonable-enquiry standard tied to named **seller** persons; never applied to title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities.

**Reasoning.** This is a constructive-knowledge bar ("discoverable from"), extends to advisers' knowledge (which is imputed across large DD teams with no individual actually aware), and has no carve-outs. It would effectively excuse the Seller from any warranty breach relating to any matter in the data room – which is the whole point of the warranties. It also directly conflicts with the DD-006 and DD-004 positions: the Buyer has "knowledge" of the incident and the Ironquay dispute, so under 8.3 it could never claim on the privacy or IP warranties even if the facts turn out far worse than disclosed.

**Position.** Delete Clause 8.3 in its entirety. Our fallback, if the Seller insists on a knowledge qualifier, is limited to the actual knowledge of two or three named Buyer deal-team individuals, no imputation of adviser knowledge, no "discoverable" standard, and express carve-outs for Title, capacity, fraud, Tax and every specific indemnity. Note the Seller's own warranty knowledge qualifiers (if any) should be the mirror image – named Seller persons after due and careful enquiry.

### 2.8 Bluefen consent – Clauses 3 / 6.3

**Seller:** "addressed"; Seller will use reasonable endeavours; consent treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

**Disclosure Letter para 2:** ~AUD 3.6m FY26 revenue (~30% of the business); consent clause 11.2, conditions in 11.3; **no final written consent and no evidence conditions are satisfied as at the date of the letter.**

**Playbook:** effective consent AND evidence that conditions are satisfied, before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavours is insufficient for a material customer.

**Reasoning.** The word "addressed" in the update draft is contradicted by the Seller's own Disclosure Letter, which confirms the consent does not exist. Bluefen is ~30% of revenue; loss of that contract would be a material impairment of the asset we are paying AUD 24m for. "Deemed satisfied on delivery" means a conditional or qualified consent (e.g. one conditioned on price concessions, re-papering or a right to terminate on change of control) would discharge the condition without the conditions in clause 11.3 being met. A "reasonable endeavours" obligation gives us no effective remedy if the Seller simply does not get there.

**Position.** Condition precedent must be: (a) written consent from Bluefen in a form approved by the Buyer (acting reasonably), unconditional or with conditions the Buyer has accepted in writing; and (b) documentary evidence that all conditions under DD-002 cl. 11.3 have been satisfied, delivered before Completion. Delete "deemed satisfied on delivery". Upgrade Seller's obligation to "all reasonable endeavours" at minimum, with information and co-operation covenants and a Buyer right to participate in Bluefen discussions. Buyer waiver right over the condition. Consider a Bluefen-specific indemnity or price mechanism if the consent is not obtained or is obtained on adverse terms – flag for commercial decision.

### 2.9 Riverlark facility – Clauses 2 / 7

**Seller:** ~AUD 3.2m outstanding; release "to be provided following Completion."

**Disclosure Letter para 3:** facility not repaid; no final discharge of security; change-of-control at cl. 8.1, discharge at cl. 9.2.

**Playbook:** current payout figure, direct repayment from Completion funds, effective security releases at Completion; a post-completion release requires an irrevocable undertaking plus Amelia Frost approval.

**Reasoning.** The deal is debt-free/cash-free. A post-completion release means the Buyer acquires a company still subject to a AUD 3.2m facility with a change-of-control trigger (cl. 8.1) and registered security over the assets. If the Seller fails to repay, the Buyer's own company is in default on day one and the Buyer has no security over the Seller for the shortfall. "Approximately AUD 3,200,000" is not a payout figure – interest, break costs and fees must be confirmed by Riverlark, not the Seller.

**Position.** Require: (a) a Riverlark payout letter dated within a short window before Completion stating the exact discharge amount; (b) that amount paid directly to Riverlark out of Completion funds under the funds flow (deducted from the price under the debt-free mechanism); (c) executed deed of release and PPSR discharge documents delivered in escrow at Completion, with registration promptly after; and (d) Riverlark's written waiver or consent in respect of cl. 8.1. If the deal team wishes to accept any post-completion element, the minimum is an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark, and it needs Amelia Frost's approval – which has not been given.

### 2.10 Employee bonuses – DD-005 and the funds flow

**Seller:** funds flow "reflects the agreed price mechanics"; AUD 420,000 bonuses "a matter for the Seller" and "not separately itemised."

**Disclosure Letter para 5:** bonuses conditional on Completion and continued employment; **not in the draft funds flow**; silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs.

**Playbook:** AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or seller-funded; the funds flow must not silently exclude them.

**Reasoning.** Bonuses triggered by Completion are a seller cost in economic substance, but the legal payer is the Company – i.e. the Buyer after Completion. If they are not in the funds flow and not treated as Debt or a price deduction, the Buyer funds them. The phrase "a matter for the Seller" is not a binding obligation. The on-cost point is real: superannuation guarantee and NSW payroll tax on AUD 420,000 could add in the order of AUD 70,000–80,000 (to be confirmed by our tax advisers – this is an estimate, not verified), and the Seller's disclosure does not address it. The "agreed price mechanics" characterisation should be rejected as a Seller assertion – nothing is agreed.

**Position.** Insert a specific funds-flow line for the DD-005 bonuses plus all associated superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs, either (a) deducted from the purchase price as Transaction Bonuses/Debt, or (b) paid by the Seller to the Company at Completion with a Seller indemnity for any shortfall. Request from the Seller the underlying bonus letters, confirmation of each recipient's continued-employment status, and a calculation of on-costs.

### 2.11 Ironquay IP indemnity – Clause 11.1

**Seller:** indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment and "considered adequate."

**Disclosure Letter para 4:** DD-004 cl. 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee; DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open but is **not** independent bank verification; no receipt and no confirmatory assignment in the data room.

**Playbook:** broaden the indemnity, preserve the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 figure is not independently verified either way.

**Reasoning.** The risk is not the AUD 180,000 payment – it is that, until the fee is paid, the Company may not own the SOW3 Project Materials at all. If those materials are embedded in the Company's product, the exposure is loss of IP ownership, third-party claims and remediation cost, none of which is covered by an indemnity limited to the fee. "Considered adequate" is the Seller's opinion. We also do not know the AUD 180,000 is right – DD-010 is the Company's own ledger.

**Position.** Broaden Clause 11.1 to an indemnity covering all Loss arising from any failure of the Company to own or have validly assigned all IP in the Ironquay deliverables (SOW1–3 and any other SOW), including third-party claims, re-development and licence costs, on a first-dollar basis, outside the general cap, basket and time limits. Preserve the cure: require the Seller to procure payment of the outstanding SOW3 fee (whatever the verified amount) and delivery of a confirmatory assignment/receipt from Ironquay before Completion as a condition or Completion deliverable. Obtain bank evidence of payment status rather than relying on either side's ledger.

### 2.12 Export/privacy incident – Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (DD-006)

**Seller:** "preliminary operational matter", "not expected to be material."

**Disclosure Letter para 6:** download link sent to an unintended external address; ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps); unknown whether accessed, exact scope unknown, notification requirement undetermined; investigation preliminary; no loss amount stated.

**Playbook:** preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction.

**Reasoning.** We should neither accept the Seller's "not material" characterisation nor overstate the issue. The honest position is that nobody yet knows. The Seller's own disclosure confirms the key facts (access, scope, notification duty) are open. The risk for us is twofold: (a) the matter could crystallise into an OAIC-notifiable breach or a Bluefen-relevant issue after Completion; and (b) under the Seller's Clause 8.3 and general disclosure, our "knowledge" of DD-006 would bar any warranty claim however the facts develop.

**Position.** Do not price or demand a number. Require: (a) a pre-Completion covenant that the Company preserve all logs, access records and the file itself; complete the investigation (including access verification with the recipient and the hosting provider); and provide written updates to the Buyer; (b) an express Buyer right to be consulted on any notification decision; (c) a specific indemnity for Loss arising from the DD-006 incident, outside the general cap, basket, time limits, Clause 8.3 and general disclosure, with the amount of actual exposure to be determined by the facts; and (d) a bring-down warranty at Completion that no further information has come to light. Reject the "not expected to be material" characterisation in the SPA drafting – the disclosure should state facts, not conclusions.

### 2.13 Sandbar renewals – DD-008 / DD-011

**Seller:** AUD 330,000 "ordinary-course operating costs."

**Disclosure Letter para 8:** three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each; does not state whether unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Playbook:** assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.

**Reasoning.** The update draft asserts "ordinary course"; the Disclosure Letter expressly refuses to say so. We should not automatically treat the AUD 330,000 as Debt, but we also should not accept the Seller's characterisation without seeing the documents. The relevant questions are timing (do they fall before or after the Locked Box / Completion accounts date?), whether they are pre-committed liabilities that should be in Working Capital or Debt, and whether DD-008 and DD-011 together reveal a single arrangement that was split.

**Position.** Request the three renewal agreements and the related DD-011 correspondence. Reserve position pending review. Ensure the price mechanism (debt-free/cash-free and any working capital adjustment) captures any accrued but unpaid element. Do not concede the "ordinary course" label in the SPA drafting; keep it as a factual matter for the price adjustment.

### 2.14 Tax and IP warranties

**Seller:** "settled under the general regime above."

**Playbook:** Tax/IP terms remain OPEN; keep categories separate; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution.

**Reasoning.** Nothing is settled. Folding Tax into an 18-month / 20% regime is inconsistent with the ATO's amendment periods (generally four years for most companies) and with a market Tax indemnity. IP, given Ironquay, is a live diligence item. Note our playbook does not require unlimited Tax liability – the ask is a separate regime, not an uncapped one.

**Position.** Reject "settled". Tax: separate Tax Indemnity and Tax Warranties with their own cap (to be agreed – the team should consider up to the purchase price) and a claims period of not less than seven years, outside basket and de minimis. IP: separate warranty set with its own cap and period, plus the Ironquay specific indemnity in 2.11. Record both expressly as open in our mark-up cover note.

### 2.15 Title evidence – DD-012

**Seller:** title evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

**Disclosure Letter para 10:** DD-012 identifies the source relied on; does not state the Buyer has verified it.

**Playbook:** independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 is a supplied internal source, not independent proof.

**Reasoning.** A share register is maintained by the Company and is prima facie, not conclusive, evidence. It will not reveal an unregistered equitable interest, a security interest over the shares, or a defect in a prior transfer. The Seller's own disclosure letter concedes it is only "the source relied on."

**Position.** Buyer to complete its own ASIC company extract and PPSR search against the Company and the Seller (shares and all assets), obtain copies of share certificates and the full chain of transfers/allotments, and require Seller board/shareholder resolutions and a solvency/authority certificate. Request confirmation that no option, pre-emption or shareholder agreement affects the shares. This verification is a Buyer action item irrespective of the SPA drafting, and the Fundamental warranty regime in 2.4 is the contractual backstop.

### 2.16 Other Disclosure Letter items (no playbook departure but note)

- **Office lease (para 7):** notification only, not consent. Confirm from DD-007 that no change-of-control default or landlord consent is triggered; add the notification as a Completion deliverable.
- **Mossvale (para 9):** restriction on assignment, not change of control. Confirm the drafting of the clause ourselves; if the contract is material, consider a warranty that no consent is required and no termination right arises from the share sale.
- **Para 1.4 (no admissions):** acceptable as a general statement, but it cannot sit alongside general disclosure – if the Seller discloses a matter, the disclosure must be specific enough to be fair (see 2.6).
- **Para 11 (reservation):** we agree; our review has proceeded on that basis.

---

## 3. Authority and escalation

| Item | Seller position | Authority status | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cap 20% / AUD 4.8m | At our fallback | **No Amelia Frost approval** | Mark back to 25%; do not reveal fallback |
| 18-month claims period | At our fallback | **No Amelia Frost approval** | Mark back to 24 months |
| Riverlark post-completion release | Below our fallback (no undertaking) | Would need Amelia Frost approval even with undertaking | Reject; require Completion payout |
| Fraud carve-out | Removed | Non-waivable | Reinstate; no authority can waive |
| Fundamental/Title regime | Collapsed into general | No fallback exists | Reject |

Recommend the deal team brief Amelia Frost now that the Seller has opened at our fallback numbers, so that if a packaged trade becomes desirable later the written authority can be obtained in advance, referencing the specific draft. This is a heads-up, not a request to use the fallbacks.

---

## 4. Summary of recommendations

**Reject and mark back:**
1. Cap to 25% / AUD 6,000,000.
2. De minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; first-dollar recovery.
3. General claims period 24 months.
4. Delete the "all Claims unless stated otherwise" default; replace with limitations applying only to General Warranty Claims.
5. Separate Fundamental/Title regime: 100% cap, ≥6 years, outside thresholds, knowledge bar and general disclosure.
6. Express non-waivable fraud / wilful concealment / deliberate misconduct carve-out from all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance.
7. Delete general data-room and public-register disclosure; specific fair disclosure only.
8. Delete Clause 8.3 blanket buyer-knowledge bar; any replacement limited to named persons' actual knowledge with full carve-outs.
9. Reject "settled" for Tax and IP; record both as open with separate regimes.

**Conditions and Completion mechanics:**
10. Bluefen: unconditional (or Buyer-approved) written consent plus evidence of cl. 11.3 conditions, before Completion; delete deemed-satisfaction; upgrade endeavours obligation.
11. Riverlark: payout letter, direct repayment from Completion funds, security releases and cl. 8.1 waiver at Completion.
12. DD-005 bonuses plus on-costs: specific funds-flow line or Seller-funded, with indemnity.
13. Ironquay: broaden the indemnity to IP ownership risk, outside the general regime; require SOW3 payment and confirmatory assignment before Completion; verify the AUD 180,000 independently.

**Diligence and information requests:**
14. DD-006: log-preservation and investigation covenants, update rights, specific indemnity, bring-down warranty; no characterisation either way.
15. Sandbar: obtain the three agreements and DD-011; assess before taking a price position.
16. Title: Buyer's own ASIC/PPSR searches, share certificates and transfer chain, authority resolutions.
17. Confirm lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) positions from source documents.

**Process:**
18. Treat every "agreed/settled/adequate/addressed" label in the Seller's package as unverified assertion; our cover note should state that no position is agreed until reflected in an executed agreement.
19. Brief Amelia Frost on the fallback-number issue; obtain no authority yet, but ensure she is aware the Seller is pitching there.

I can turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up schedule or a cover letter to Seller's counsel if that is the next step.
